result:
Quick check of the three answers: solution 1 gives 1/2, solution 2 gives 3/8, and solution 3 gives 1/4. I believe the true limit is 1/3, so none is correct.

**Upper bound h ≤ n/3.** Holes must be pairwise king-separated: two holes that share a corner violate boundary disjointness. Every cell in the 3×3 neighbourhood of a hole must be in P, since a hole's orthogonal neighbours must be in P and a diagonal cell that is not in P would put a corner of the hole on the outer boundary. Each hole lies in four 2×2 blocks, and each such block contains at most one hole. Each block containing a hole therefore has three other cells, all in P. That gives 4h blocks with 3 P-cells each, so 12h incidences. Each cell lies in at most four 2×2 blocks, so |P| ≥ 12h/4 = 3h.

**Construction achieving 1/3.** Take the rectangle [−1, 2a−1] × [−1, 2b−1] and remove the cells (2i, 2j) for 0 ≤ i < a, 0 ≤ j < b. The remaining cells form a connected polyomino with n = 3ab + 2a + 2b + 1 cells and h = ab holes. Each hole is a single cell with its 8 neighbours in P, and the hole boundaries are pairwise disjoint and disjoint from the outer boundary. So h/n → 1/3.

The solutions that reach other values make errors. Solution 3's Lemma 1 is false: two holes can share a neighbouring P-cell on opposite sides, since their boundary edges are distinct. Solution 2 overlooks that the (odd, odd) cells in its lattice would be enclosed holes touching the existing holes at corners, so they cannot be left out of P.

CHOICE: NONE
CONFIDENCE: 4
